scenes.intro: Hello, Michael. You want two things: to buy a home in 2027 and to retire at 58. Your score is 26 out of 100, which Sherpas calls critical. That sounds hard, but you start from strength: you save $43,000 a year. The problem is that the same dollars are being asked to do too many jobs at once.
scenes.pillar_savings_and_cash_flow: Your plumbing, your savings and cash flow, is broken. You save well, but each year about $8,336 more goes out than comes in. Retirement, the home and your cash cushion all pull on the same income.
scenes.pillar_debt: Your walls, your debt, are solid. What you owe is manageable. The one to watch is a $3,500 credit card at 20%: small, but your most expensive debt.
scenes.pillar_investments: Your garden, your investments, is cracked. You have $145,000 invested, but less of it is in stocks than the growth plan you chose. At 37, that gap can cost you years of growth.
scenes.pillar_liquidity_and_emergency_fund: Your foundations, your emergency cash, are broken. You have $30,000 set aside, $16,530 short of the minimum cushion we suggest. And the home purchase in January 2027 would use up that cash.
scenes.pillar_insurance_and_protection: Your roof, your insurance, is broken. Your life cover is $720,000 short of what is recommended, and you have no umbrella policy. If something went wrong, the savings you are building would be exposed.
scenes.move_1: The easiest step is umbrella insurance: $1M of extra cover in case someone makes a big claim against you. It takes your score from 26 to 31.
scenes.move_2: The biggest step is about later: plan to take less out of your savings each year once you retire, so they last longer. On its own, it takes your score from 26 to 62, the largest jump of the three.
scenes.move_3: The third step: put more of your invested money in stocks, closer to the growth mix you chose, moving about $19,900. It takes your score from 26 to 31.
scenes.timeline: Now the years ahead. You plan to retire at 58. On today's plan, your savings run out at 85, six years before the plan ends at 91. After that you would rely mostly on Social Security. That trade-off is the one to talk through with your advisor.

simple.intro: Michael, your financial health score is 26 out of 100. Let's walk through your home room by room to see what is strong and what needs work.
simple.pillar_savings_and_cash_flow: Your plumbing is savings and cash flow, and it is broken. It scores 0 out of 25, so there is little spare cash each month.
simple.pillar_debt: Your walls are debt, and they are solid. They score 8 out of 10. Your debts are small compared to your income.
simple.pillar_investments: Your garden is investments, and it is cracked. It scores 11 out of 25. Most of your money is there, so it matters.
simple.pillar_liquidity_and_emergency_fund: Your foundations are your emergency fund and cash, and they are broken. They score 4 out of 20. You have less set aside than is safe.
simple.pillar_insurance_and_protection: Your roof is insurance and protection, and it is broken. It scores 4 out of 20. You have little cover if something goes wrong.
simple.move_1: Your plan adds umbrella cover, which protects you if someone sues you. It repairs your roof and lifts your score to 31 out of 100.
simple.move_2: Your plan takes less money out of savings each year. This repairs your plumbing and lifts the score to 62 out of 100.
simple.move_3: Your plan moves more of your long term money into stocks. This repairs your garden and lifts the score to 31 out of 100.
simple.timeline: Your savings run out at age 85 on this plan. Your debts get paid off along the way, but later spending goes unpaid.

numbers.intro: Michael, your financial health score is 26 out of 100, which is critical. That means your income is doing several jobs at once and the plan has real gaps.
numbers.pillar_savings_and_cash_flow: Your savings and cash flow score is 0 out of 25, and your plumbing is broken. You save $43,000 a year, but cash flow is about $8,336 a year short. Your $30,000 cash covers 3.2 months and is $16,530 short of the $46,530 low reserve, so a surprise expense hits before saving for later can.
numbers.pillar_debt: Your debt score is 8 out of 10, and your walls are solid. Total debt is $28,500, but the $3,500 card at 20% costs you most. That card is projected to clear by July 2028 only if $200 a month keeps going, and your $30,000 cash is $16,530 short of the $46,530 low reserve.
numbers.pillar_investments: Your investments score is 11 out of 25, and your garden is cracked. You hold $145,000 invested, but 73.5% in stocks against a 98% target. That gap means your money is taking less growth than the plan assumes, while $24,000 a year keeps going in.
numbers.pillar_liquidity_and_emergency_fund: Your emergency fund score is 4 out of 20, and your foundations are broken. Your $30,000 cash covers 3.2 months of $9,306 in monthly expenses, $16,530 short of the $46,530 low reserve. After the $113,300 home purchase and $3,500 vacation, that cash covers 0 months.
numbers.pillar_insurance_and_protection: Your insurance and protection score is 4 out of 20, and your roof is broken. You have $180,000 of life insurance against a recommended $900,000 to $1,800,000, a $720,000 shortfall. With no extra cover for large claims, a claim beyond your $172,000 of liquid assets could reach your $218,500 net worth.
numbers.move_1: This takes your score from 26 to 31 out of 100. You would add $1M of cover for large claims against you, a repair for your roof.
numbers.move_2: This takes your score from 26 to 62 out of 100. You would take less out of your savings each year in retirement, down to $10,300 a year, which is 6.0%. That repairs your plumbing.
numbers.move_3: This takes your score from 26 to 31 out of 100. You would move more of your invested savings toward growth, from 74% to 88%, about $19,900. That repairs your garden.
numbers.timeline: Your savings and investments run out at age 85. You plan to retire at 58, and the plan has your debts paid off by 2057. That leaves the years after 85 without the savings the plan relies on.
